newsitem.title: JAPAN: Businessmen leave to check N.Korea free-trade zone.
newsitem.headline: Businessmen leave to check N.Korea free-trade zone.

text.p: Asian, European and American business executives on Wednesday headed for North Korea at the invitation of the communist state to investigate its fledgling attempt to create a capitalist free-trade area.
"We going to check out conditions in the North Korea free-trade zone," said a Japanese businessman from an electronics company, who declined to be identified.
"I think the success of this forum is important. It is one of the last chances for North Korea to succeed economically," he said.
"The economy in North Korea really at the bottom. It cannot get any worse," he said.

He was one of 145 business leaders travelling by ship from this Japanese port to Rajin-Sonbong, located on the Tumen river near North Korea's border with China and Russia to attend a three-day forum organised by the United Nations Development Programme.
They will be joined by about 100 business executives who are flying from Beijing.
But the success of the trip was put in doubt on Tuesday when Seoul, upset by the exclusion of its officials and journalists from the trip, pulled out of the forum.
North Korea invited a representative of the Korea Federation of Small Business and 24 businessmen, most from small companies.
Seoul had asked for 53 places and maintains North Korea agreed to welcome anyone who wanted to attend.
The attempt by Pyongyang to attract investment to what it hopes will be a Chinese-style foreign investment window comes as its foreign trade has collapsed.

The country is on the brink of famine, caused by widespread flooding last year and further floods this year, and desperately needs investment in export industries to earn hard currency for purchases of food and fuel.
North Korea watchers believe a boycott will seriously damage economic ties between North and South Korea, still technically at war following their 1950-53 conflict.
South Korean businessmen take their lead on North Korean investments from their government, and so far the message has been to risk nothing.
North Korea is offering 101 industrial projects in Rajin-Sonbong and is hoping to attract $800 million in investment.
The projects range from a semiconductor plant and an oil refinery to factories making furniture and toys.

The remote zone lacks basic port and transport infrastructure, and Pyongyang has no money to pay for it. So far the area boasts only two investors -- a Swedish individual and a Chinese shipping company.
The business executives on the ship included banker Keith Chiddy, who is based in Pyongyang.

"We are interested in who is on this ship because we want to know who wants to work constructively to do business with North Korea," said Chiddy, general manager of ING North East Asia Bank, one of two foreign banks operating in North Korea.
The other bank is Peregine-Daesong Development Bank, which is a joint venture involving Hong Kong's Peregrine Investments Holdings Ltd.
